This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set such that $\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert=o(x^{1/2})$. Let\[B=\{ n\geq 1 : a\nmid n\textrm{ for all }a\in A\}.\]If $B=\{b_1<b_2<\cdots\}$ then is it true that\[\lim \frac{1}{x}\sum_{b_i<x}(b_{i+1}-b_i)^2\]exists (and is finite)?
#489: [Er61]
number theory
For example, when $A=\{p^2: p\textrm{ prime}\}$ then $B$ is the set of squarefree numbers, and the existence of this limit was proved by Erdős. 
See also [208].

A full proof 
claimed by Colin Snyder (using GPT 5.6 (custom harness)).
 Summary:
 We claim the answer is yes: for every $A$ with $|A\cap[1,x]|=o(\sqrt{x})$, the limit of $\frac{1}{x}\sum_{b_i<x}(b_{i+1}-b_i)^2$ exists and is finite. Proved in Lean 4 / Mathlib, standard axioms only, no sorry.
Idea: finite versions of the sieve are periodic, so their gap statistics converge on their own; the only danger is squared mass escaping into ever-longer gaps. We make every long gap pay a charge: inside any long gap, positions $n\equiv 1\pmod{Y!}$ supply many candidates, each blocked by a distinct large element of $A$, and after removing shared prime factors a gap of length $G$ yields on the order of $G^2$ coprime witness pairs. A lattice-geometry bound caps the total charge each pair of elements of $A$ can receive over all gaps at once, and that total is a convergent double sum. So long gaps carry uniformly little squared mass and the periodic limits converge to the true limit.
 Notes:
 Verify: unzip, build with the included checker, then "#print axioms" on the final theorem gives exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. The bundle includes a statement-fidelity audit (open intervals, exact gap squares, limit over real cutoffs).
